2530.dq: However, Kwami, a Chadic language spoken in Nigeria, is described by Leger (1994) as having stress in words that lack vowel length and High tone. ... stress is also heard on the final syllable of words lacking High tones or long vowels.
2530.heavy: syllables with a long vowel are always stressed and initial High toned syllables or closed syllables also attract stress (when there is no long vowel)
2530.dflt: final syllable (kùrè 'caveat'); but an initial High-toned syllable (kábá 'inside') or a closed syllable (kòmkáy 'pluck', stressed closed syllable word-initial) takes the stress before the final default applies
2530.prule: A syllable with a long vowel is stressed wherever it stands in the word (háakù, gàrìngáalè); if the word has no long vowel, an initial High-toned syllable or a closed syllable takes the stress (kábá, kòmkáy). Downing's wording 'initial High toned syllables or closed syllables also attract stress' leaves open whether 'initial' also restricts the closed-syllable term; the only closed-syllable example, kòmkáy, has its stressed closed syllable word-initially, so both readings fit the data. A word with neither a long vowel, nor an initial High tone, nor a (relevant) closed syllable is stressed on the final syllable (kùrè).

2530.tone: Tone language ('Chadic languages are all tonal'). The stress statement is additional to tone and partly tone-conditioned: with no long vowel, an initial H-toned syllable attracts stress (kábá). In kòmkáy the initial closed L syllable is stressed while the final syllable carries H; since only initial High-toned syllables are said to attract stress, the final H is not a candidate under the rule as relayed, so the example shows that a non-initial H does not draw stress, not that closure outranks H. Downing frames reported Chadic 'stress' as possibly a European-ear artefact of H tone plus length (Wolff 1993, Dresel 1977 on Hausa) and presents Kwami as the counter-case where stress is heard on syllables lacking both; she calls for phonetic study (p. 110).
2530.sec_quote: These points are illustrated by the data below (accents indicate tones; the stressed syllable is underlined): (5) Kwami stress (Leger 1994, pp 91-92) háakù 'yawn (noun)' gàrìngáalè 'bicycle, wheel' kábá 'inside' kòmkáy 'pluck' kùrè 'fence' ... Clearly more phonetic studies of the correlates of stress in Chadic languages are necessary to disentangle this controversy.

2532.tone: Dammann p. 8 treats pitch (Tonhöhe) as lexically distinctive but under-investigated, giving six minimal pairs (eguru 'sky'/'leg', mphango 'stick'/'will', mphuku 'mouse'/'arm muscle', ndi 'fly'/'or', sidira 'taboo'/'bird', zera 'winnow'/'be bright'); pitch and accent are notated only sporadically. Legère 2025 (Oxford Guide to the Bantu Languages, p. 896; excerpt grade only): 'Kwangali is a tone language. The study of its tonal structure is rudimentary. The high tone of lexical items (often found on penultimate syllables)14 and grammatical forms is marked by an acute accent in this chapter, while low tone remains unmarked. There are only a few lexical items where the distinctive function of tone has been demonstrated.' Sommer 2003 (Routledge Bantu Languages p. 571, in the copy consulted elsewhere) reports that some deny tone is distinctive in the Kavango group. So the language is tonal AND has a stated stem-anchored stress rule; tone or pitch accent is the alternative coding if the verifier holds that Dammann's hedged footnote is not a stress rule.

2536.prule: No fixed stress pattern; stress 'commonly' penultimate, stated per word length as tendencies with lexical exceptions in every class: 2-syll usually initial (but pa'ngae); 3-syll usually medial (but 'kenapa, 'pokota, 'uruwai, 'rambulyu, 'lasaka, reduplicated 'kilyipu 'kilyipu, 'kapara 'kapara initial); 4-syll primary on the third with possible subsidiary stress on the first (but 'alemakai, ku'lumbulyu, pa'kalepa, ya'ngalana); longer forms (often compounded verbs) usually main stress on the fourth syllable (but pya'kalyamano, pi'pyamopape). Proper names follow no strict rules. Stress position is lexically contrastive in at least two recorded pairs: 'kyakapya 'he became well' vs kya'kapya 'he became mad' (entry kyakalyamo), and kyasilyu (initial stress) vs kasilyu (second-syllable stress).

2537.tone: Three level tones H, M, L (Platiel 1982 p. 91; independently Jones 2010 p. 11: 'Every syllable in the Kyanga language has a tone... There are 3 level tones - high (H), mid (M) and (L)'). Platiel says the tone levels do not seem to co-occur with a stress accent; Jones 2010 says nothing about stress (its 'accent' hits are orthographic tone marks only). Tones are altered by morpho-syntactic conditioning (verb tense marked by tone); long vowels show rising contours; base tones of most lexemes not yet established in 1982 so tones are mostly unmarked in the article.

2538.prule: No word stress. 2545.tone: Three level tones (ton haut, moyen, bas); the author marks tone only where syntactic function changes it (verbal substantive raising the verb vowel's tone: tee fú'fu vs tee fu wa). Footnote 3 and the p. 24 talking-drum passage confirm that every syllable is beaten on one of the three tones. An 'accent d'intensité' on 'certaines syllabes des mots' is asserted, with reduction/loss of unaccented syllables as its diagnostic (initial vowel in bĕleda > bleda, final vowels in temŏ > tem, marœ̆ > mar), but no position is given; p. 19 adds that œ is frequent 'surtout dans des syllabes peu accentuées'. A full-text search (accent/intensit/abrèg/syllabe) finds no other prosodic passage in the book.

2546.prule: Final-syllable stress in every non-monosyllabic word (and phrase): the last syllable is the 'primary syllable' with full stress and the full range of vowel-length and lexical-tone contrasts; all pre-final syllables are reduced (unstressed, atonal, no length contrast), e.g. sesquisyllabic kabùang4 'ceramic tile' = reduced ka- + stressed -bùang4. Position is set by syllable count alone (right edge); no weight or segmental condition.

2551.prule: Stress ('acento') is lexical: roots and affixes are underlyingly accented or not (marked per morpheme in Telles's underlying forms), and the position of primary stress in the word follows from which morphemes carry lexical accent -- accented root /ˈna̰n-ˈte/ -> [ˈna̰:ˌde] 'blood' (root primary, suffix secondary) vs unaccented root of the same CVN shape /a̰n-ˈte/ -> [ˌa̰:ˈnde] 'wasp' (referential suffix -te takes primary). Pitch (H on stressed, L on unstressed) is the phonetic correlate; Telles calls it a pitch-accent system.
2551.srule: When a word carries more than one lexical accent (or none), the leftmost stress is primary and all the others are secondary (Costa 2020: 308, 313): other lexically accented morphemes (e.g. referential -te, imperfective -tãn) and, root-internally, the second heavy syllable of a root with two heavies (phonetic secondary) or the final syllable of a trisyllabic root whose heavy initial takes primary. Second-hand (Costa 2020 summarising Telles 2002); Telles 2012 states no secondary rule but marks ˌ in her transcriptions ([ˈna̰:ˌde] /ˈna̰n-ˈte/, [ˈṵ̃:ˌndã̰ˌna̰] /ˈṵ̃n-ˈtãn-ˈna̰/, p.295; where the only lexical accent is on a suffix after an unaccented root her marks vary: [ˌa̰:ˈnde] /a̰n-ˈte/ and [ˌã:ˈdãn] /ãn-ˈtãn/ p.295, but [kãˈma̰:ˌRãna] /ka-ma̰h-ˈtãn-ta/ p.296 ex.04). tn.quote: Em nível prosódico, o correlato fonético do acento é o tom (pitch), constituindo um sistema prosódico conhecido na literatura como pitch accent. tn.translation: At the prosodic level, the phonetic correlate of the accent is pitch, constituting a prosodic system known in the literature as pitch accent. The accent is lexical, and combined with it is the metrical accent, sensitive to syllable weight. In addition, there is a level tone that operates in morphophonological processes.

2554.dq: Secara fonetis tekanan kata bahasa Lawangan terdapat pada suku kedua dari belakang .
2554.dloc: p. 26, Bab III Fonologi, sec. 3.6 'Fonem Suprasegmental' (Google Books vol. 7MYtAAAAMAAJ excerpt indexed PA26; p.26 is absent from the held kemdikbud scan).
2554.heavy: Only one condition is stated: a penult whose vowel is /ə/ loses the stress ('Tekanan berubah kalau pada suku kedua dari belakang terda- pat vokal / ə /'). No coda or vowel-length condition; geminate vowels /jaa/ 'village', /soo/ 'wound' are said (sec. 3.4.2, p.24, in the scan) to be 'diucapkan dengan tekanan pada vokal pertama', i.e. still the penult. 2554.dflt: Penult when the penult vowel is full (the general statement). When the penult is /ə/ the stress 'changes' -- final in the disyllabic examples /belay/, /emmaq/; words with schwa in both syllables and words longer than two syllables with a schwa penult (e.g. /tempun/, /kerewaw/ in the example list, whose stress marks the excerpt text does not carry) are not addressed in the text available.
2554.prule: Word stress is non-phonemic ('secara fonetis'; stress, pitch, length and pause do not distinguish meaning) and falls on the penultimate syllable ('suku kedua dari belakang'); if the penult vowel is /ə/ the stress shifts ('tekanan berubah'), e.g. /belay/ 'house', /emmaq/ 'father' -- in these disyllabic examples necessarily onto the final syllable; the landing site is not stated in words.

2555.idn: Nagarige (Capell: 'Nagarige (Banoni)', 'Banoni N.'), with its Amun dialect ('the Amu[n] village dialect of Nagarige'); west coast of Bougainville, shores of Empress Augusta Bay
2555.exq_: but here the Amun dialect has vi- lisuna, ‘his nose’, and vi'suuna, ‘her breast’. It is clear, therefore, that these languages call for further study while they are still available. (no rule is stated; Capell's own Amun forms are offered as a complication to the stress reading)
2555.tone: No tone or pitch-accent mentioned for Nagarige/Amun. Lincoln 1976 (PL A-45, p. 79 letter-spaced: 'P i t ch and s t re s s are not marked. Repeat e d l e t t e r s r e p re s ent long vowe l s or na s a l s.') says of his Piva/Banoni orthography only that pitch and stress are not marked and that doubled letters mark long vowels or nasals.
2555.sec_quote: the -na third person sin- gular ending of nouns in the vocabulary, there are no examples of other persons, so that the completeness of the system in these languages cannot be determined as yet. It would seem that stress can be phonemic here, as the Nagarige vocabulary gives 'yisuna, ‘his nose’, as against vi'suna, ‘her breast’, but here the Amun dialect has vi- lisuna, ‘his nose’, and vi'suuna, ‘her breast’.

2555.cfw: Capell 1971 only suggested from his 1963 survey wordlists that stress might be phonemic in Nagarige (ˈvisuna 'his nose' vs viˈsuna 'her breast') while himself recording the Amun forms with a vowel-length difference, Lincoln 1975, working first-hand in all four Banoni-Piva varieties, found no word distinguished by stress or pitch and treats vowel length as the contrast, and neither says where stress falls, so nothing about Lawunuia stress placement is known.
